en: The Sūtra on the Auspicious Response of the Prince’s Original Arising, Volume One, translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu Dynasty.
The Buddha said: “I recall my own past lives; at a time countless kalpas ago, I was originally an ordinary person.”
Since first seeking the Buddha-way, his spirit has taken on forms, cycling through all five realms of existence.
As one body perishes, another is received; thus, births and deaths have been immeasurable.
Suppose all the grasses and trees under heaven were cut down to be made into counting-slips; even these could not suffice to count my former bodies.
"The period from the beginning to the end of heaven and earth is called one kalpa, yet the number of times I have undergone the formation and destruction of heaven and earth cannot be recorded."

Therefore, moved by compassion for the world whose greedy intentions flow on endlessly, submerged in the ocean of craving and desire, I alone wish to return to its source; thus, I exert myself and emerge from it.
Therefore, throughout successive generations, they have labored diligently without regarding it as toil;
they have kept their minds empty, delighting in stillness, practicing non-action and freedom from desire;

they have diminished themselves to practice giving, maintained the precepts with utmost sincerity, remained humble and patient, and exerted themselves with courageous diligence, focusing their thoughts on the subtle to study the sagely wisdom.

He brings life to the world through benevolence; he pities the destitute and laments those in distress; he consoles and soothes the sorrowful; he nurtures all sentient beings and rescues those in suffering; he serves the Buddhas and the uniquely awakened True Persons; his accumulated merits are such that they cannot be fully recorded.

In the past, when Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world, there was a holy king named Jayasena who ruled over the great kingdom of Pāṭaliputra; the people were long-lived and happy, and the world was at peace.
At that time, I was a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta;
from childhood I possessed wisdom, and my aspirations were vast and magnanimous. I lived in seclusion among mountains and marshes, guarding the profound mystery and practicing dhyāna.
Hearing that there was a Buddha in the world, his heart was filled with singular joy; donning a deer-skin robe, he set out to enter the kingdom.
On his way, he passed through a village settlement where there were five hundred practitioners of the Way.
The Bodhisattva surpassed them, discoursing on the Way and explaining its principles throughout the day and night; both teacher and disciples were filled with joy.
When it was time for their parting, each of the five hundred people presented him with a silver coin, which the Bodhisattva accepted.
"Entering the city and seeing the people, he was filled with joy and hurried along; they were leveling and repairing the roads, sprinkling water, sweeping clean, and burning incense.
He immediately asked a passerby:
'For what purpose is this being done?'"
The traveler replied,
"Today the Buddha shall come into the city.
The Bodhisattva was greatly delighted and thought to himself:
"How wonderful!
Now that I have been able to see the Buddha, I shall seek my vow.
At that very moment, a maiden of the royal house passed by; her name was Gopī. She carried a water pitcher and held seven blue lotuses.
The Bodhisattva pursued her and called out,
"Sister, please stop!
I would like to hire the flower in your hand for a hundred silver coins."
The woman said, “The Buddha is about to enter the city; the King has fasted, purified himself with ritual bathing, and wishes to offer flowers to him, but they cannot be obtained.
She requested again, saying:
"Sister, you may seek more.
When she refused to accept even two hundred or three hundred coins as wages, he immediately reached into his bag and gave her all five hundred silver coins.

Gopī thought of flowers; though they were extremely cheap, costing only a few coins, she hired [the vendor] for five hundred [pieces]. Greedy for his silver treasure, she gave him five stalks of flowers and kept two for herself.
He turned his mind aside with doubt, thinking:
"What kind of Daoist is this, wearing a deer-skin robe that barely covers his body, yet not sparing silver coins or treasures to obtain these five stalks of flowers?"
Overjoyed and unusual in his demeanor, he called out after him:
"O man! Tell me the truth, and these flowers may be obtained; [otherwise, you shall die]."
"Otherwise, I shall seize you.
The Bodhisattva looked back and said, "I purchased these flowers for between one hundred and five hundred coins to offer as a personal gift; why should you seek to seize them?"
The woman said, "I am a member of the royal family; my power is sufficient to seize you.
The Bodhisattva remained silent and said:
"I wish to offer this to the Buddha, seeking only the fulfillment of my aspirations. Gopī said,
"Excellent!"
"I vow that in future lives, I shall always be your wife, never parting from you whether in beauty or ugliness;
I shall keep this in my heart so that the Buddha may know it.
Now, as I am weak and unable to come forward, I beg to entrust these two flowers to be offered to the Buddha."
The Bodhisattva consented.
"In a short while the Buddha arrived; the king, his ministers, and the people all came forward to welcome and pay their respects, each scattering famous flowers, which all fell upon the ground."
When the Bodhisattva beheld the Buddha, he scattered five stalks of flowers; they all remained suspended in mid-air, appearing as if rooted directly above the Buddha, with none falling to the ground.
He then scattered two more flowers, which likewise stayed suspended on either side of the Buddha’s shoulders.
The Buddha, knowing his sincere intention, praised the Bodhisattva, saying:

"Throughout incalculable kalpas, that which you have studied has been pure; you have subdued your mind and cast aside your life, renounced desire to maintain emptiness, and attained non-arising and non-ceasing. Through your compassion free from dependence, and by accumulating meritorious deeds and vows, you have now realized this."
He then made a prediction concerning him, saying:

"From this point forward, after ninety-one kalpas, in an eon named Bhadra, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. In the language of India, 'Śākya' means 'able' and 'muni' means 'sage'; thus, the meaning of the name is 'Able Sage'."
“When the Bodhisattva had received the words of prediction, his doubts were resolved and his expectations ceased;
suddenly free from conceptual thought, he entered meditative absorption in stillness.

He immediately attained the pure *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the forbearance that phenomena do not arise), whereupon he rose lightly into the air to a height of seven *zhang* above the ground. Descending from above, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet.”

Seeing that the ground was soaked and muddy, he immediately took off his deerskin garment, intending to cover it; however, it was insufficient to mask the mud. He then untied his hair and spread it upon the ground, requesting the Buddha to tread upon it as he passed by.
The Buddha further declared:

"Because you are so diligent and courageous, when you attain Buddhahood in the future, you shall deliver all devas and humans in an age of five turbidities without regarding it as difficult; you shall surely be like me."
"The Bodhisattva served Dīpaṃkara until his parinirvāṇa.
Upholding the precepts and protecting the Dharma, at the end of his life he was reborn in the first heaven above as one of the Four Heavenly Kings."

Having completed his full lifespan in heaven, he was reborn in the human realm as a Cakravartin, a Universal Monarch who travels through the air—possessing the seven treasures that appeared spontaneously: first, the golden wheel treasure; second, the divine jewel treasure; third, the dark-blue horse treasure with crimson mane and tail; fourth, the white elephant treasure with crimson mane and tail; fifth, the jade woman treasure; sixth, the wise minister treasure; and seventh, the holy counselor treasure. After eighty-four thousand years, at the end of his life, he immediately ascended to be born in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa, as Śakra, Lord of Devas.
When his lifespan ended, he ascended again to the seventh Brahma Heaven and became a Brahmā King.
In this manner, he alternately served as the Lord of Devas above and as a Sage Sovereign below, each for thirty-six cycles, repeating this process over and over.

As for his transformations, they manifest according to the times; sometimes he becomes a sagely sovereign, and sometimes he acts as a patriarch of the Confucian scholars, a national preceptor, or a Daoist master—his manifestations wherever he appears are beyond reckoning or record.

"For ninety-one kalpas, the Bodhisattva cultivated the Way and its virtue, studied the Buddha's intent, and mastered the practices of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). He was then in the position of being one birth away from Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
Subsequently, he was reborn in the fourth heaven above, Tuṣita, where he served as the teacher of the devas; his merit was perfected, his resolve fulfilled, and his divine wisdom immeasurable."

When the destined time arrived, he was to become a Buddha immediately; he took birth in the kingdom of Kapilavastu in India, where his father, King Śuddhodana, was wise, benevolent, and virtuous, and his consort, Queen Māyā, was chaste, righteous, gentle, and kind.
Kapilavastu is the center of the three thousand suns and moons and the twelve thousand heavens and earths.

The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is most supreme and most profound; he cannot be born in a peripheral land, for such lands would cause the earth to tilt and slant. Therefore, he dwells in its very center.
Transforming throughout the ten directions, all the Buddhas who arose in antiquity emerged from this very place.
When the Bodhisattva first descended, he manifested riding a white elephant, his crown radiant with the essence of the sun.
Because his mother was napping during the day, he manifested himself in a dream, entering through her right side.
When the lady awoke from her dream, she realized for herself that she was pregnant; the King immediately summoned the chief diviner to interpret her dream.
The hexagram says:
"Where the Way and its Virtue converge, the world receives their blessings; one must surely cherish the Sage Child.
While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, he was pure and free from any foul odor or impurity.
Thereupon, when the ministers and the various minor kings heard that the Great King’s consort was pregnant, they all came to offer their congratulations.
While in the womb, the Bodhisattva saw the outsiders prostrating; as if looking through fine gauze, he secretly brushed them away with his hand.
The intention of those who ward off [these offerings] is not to disturb others.

From the moment a woman conceives, Heaven provides her with food and drink that arrive naturally; she receives and enjoys them without knowing their origin, and thus she no longer partakes of the royal kitchen, considering it bitter and pungent.

On the night of the eighth day of the fourth month, when the morning star appeared, he was born from his mother’s right side through transformation. Upon touching the ground, he immediately took seven steps, raised his right hand, and stood there, saying:
"In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am the most honored."
"The three realms are all suffering; what is there that can be enjoyed?
At that moment, heaven and earth shook violently, and the palace was filled with light.
Brahmā, Śakra, and the devas descended from mid-air to attend upon him.
The Four Heavenly Kings received him and placed him upon a golden pedestal, bathing the Prince’s body with celestial fragrant water.

His body was the color of gold and possessed the thirty-two marks; its radiance shone forth, reaching upward to the twenty-eighth heaven and downward to the eighteen hells, such that within the entire realm of the Buddhas there was no place not illuminated by its great light.
On that night, thirty-two auspicious omens descended from heaven:
first, the earth shook greatly and all ruins were leveled; second, the streets and alleys became naturally pure and foul-smelling places turned fragrant;
third, all withered trees within the kingdom’s borders sprouted flowers and leaves; fourth, the gardens...
Fifth, marvelous and sweet fruits grow spontaneously in the gardens; sixth, lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels grow upon the land;
seventh, hidden treasures from within the earth all emerge of their own accord;
eighth, the precious objects stored therein appear clearly and brilliantly; ninth, chests and garments are already spread out upon the racks.
10. The myriad rivers and ten thousand streams become still and clear; 11. The winds subside and the clouds disperse, leaving the sky bright and serene;
12. The heavens send down a fine rain from all four directions that moistens with fragrance;
13. A divine moon-jewel is suspended in the hall; 14. The lamps and torches within the palace are no longer used.
15. The sun, moon, and stars all came to a standstill and ceased their movement;
16. the constellation Puṣya descended to attend the birth of the Prince; 17. the gods of the eight directions brought precious jewels to present as offerings;
18. celestial food of a hundred flavors appeared spontaneously before him; 19. [and so forth].
Twenty: Ten thousand mouths of precious jars hang suspended, filled with sweet nectar; twenty-one: Divine beings arrive drawing a seven-jeweled lattice-canopied chariot;
twenty-two: Five hundred white elephant cubs spontaneously appear and stand arrayed before the palace;
twenty-three: Five hundred white lion cubs emerge from the Snowy Mountains and stand arrayed at the city gate.
21) Celestial maidens appeared upon the shoulders of courtesans; 22) daughters of the nāga kings stood encircling the palace;
23) ten thousand celestial jade maidens held peacock-feather whisks and appeared upon the palace walls;
24) celestial maidens holding golden vases filled with fragrant liquid stood in rows in mid-air.
27. All the celestial music descended and played simultaneously; 28.
All the hells ceased their torments and poisonous pains no longer afflicted beings; 29. Venomous insects hid away while auspicious birds soared and sang;
30. Fishermen and hunters, along with all those harboring malice and hatred, suddenly gave rise to hearts of compassion; 31. Within the realm, those who were pregnant...
All women who have given birth shall bear sons; those suffering from deafness, blindness, muteness, lameness, or any of the hundred ailments shall all be completely healed and restored;
thirty-second, tree spirits shall manifest in human form, bowing their heads in reverent service.
At that time, everyone in the surrounding area was filled with refined wonder and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
The lady immediately wrapped him in white cloth, and a wet nurse took him to raise him, naming him Siddhārtha.
The King said to his consort:

"This son who has been born is no ordinary being. In our kingdom there is a man of the Way named Āyu, over a hundred years of age, a venerable elder of great learning who clearly understands the science of physiognomy.
Would it be acceptable for us to go together now to have him examine the child?"
The lady said, "Excellent!

She immediately prepared a carriage drawn by a white elephant, with attendants and musical performances, and went out to visit the practitioner. She offered him one bag each of gold and silver, but the practitioner would not accept them.
When the Prince was stripped of his garments, thirty-two marks were seen upon him: his body was golden in color; he had a fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head;

his hair was deep blue-black; between his eyebrows was a white tuft of hair; his neck possessed the radiance of sunlight; the eyelids of his eyes were deep blue; both upper and lower lashes blinked simultaneously; his mouth had forty teeth, which were white, even, and level; his jawbones were square and broad; his tongue was long enough to reach his hairline; his chest was full like that of a lion; his body was perfectly upright; his arms and fingers were long; the heels of his feet were full and level with the soles; his hands could grasp both inside and out; his palms and fingers were joined by a web-like membrane; the soles of his feet bore the pattern of a thousand-spoked wheel; his male organ was retracted within a sheath like that of a horse; his calves were like those of a deer; his bones were linked together like a chain; his body hair curled to the right; from each pore grew a single hair; his skin and hair were fine and soft, repelling dust and water; and upon his breast was the mark of a svastika.
Seeing this, Ārāḍa increased his sighs and shed tears; overcome with grief, he could not speak.
The King’s consort was afraid and, bowing with her hands joined, asked:
"Is there some omen of ill fortune?"
"Please tell me its meaning.
Raising his hand, he replied,
"Auspiciousness without anything unfavorable!"
I venture to congratulate the Great King on having given birth to this divine person.
That the heavens and earth shook violently last night was precisely for this reason.
My method of interpreting signs states:

"If a king begets a son who possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, he shall, while residing in his kingdom, become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents. The seven treasures will come to him spontaneously; he can fly as he walks; weapons are not used, and peace and prosperity prevail naturally."
"If one does not delight in the world but abandons home to practice the Way, they shall become a Buddha by nature and deliver all the people.

It is because I am grieved that my years are already late in life and I am about to pass into the next world; I shall not behold the arising of a Buddha nor hear his sutras, and for this reason I lament for myself."

The King, deeply aware of his skill in physiognomy, built palaces for him and constructed three seasonal halls, each in a separate location—a hall for autumn during the rainy season, a hall for coolness during the summer heat, and a hall for warmth during the cold and snow. He selected five hundred courtesans, choosing those who were upright in appearance, neither fat nor thin, neither tall nor short, neither too fair nor too dark, and possessed of clever talents;

each was accompanied by several attendants. All were adorned with necklaces of white pearls and famous jewels, and they served in shifts of one hundred at a time to provide him with constant attendance.

In front of the palace, sweet fruit trees were planted in rows, with bathing ponds interspersed among them. Within the ponds were rare flowers and birds of various kinds numbering in the thousands; their magnificent adornments and brilliant plumage delighted the Prince’s mind, intending to dissuade him from seeking the Way.
The palace walls were solid and secure, and the sound of the gates opening and closing could be heard for forty li.
On the day the Prince was born, a maidservant of the royal house also gave birth to a male slave, a white colt was born in the stables, and a yellow lamb was born as well.
The slave’s name was Chandaka, and the horse’s name was Kanthaka.
Later, the King constantly employed Chandaka as his attendant and provided the white horse for his transport.

"Seven days after his birth, his mother passed away; because she had conceived the Teacher of Gods and Men, her merit and blessings were so great that she was reborn above in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where she received its natural rewards."
The Bodhisattva, knowing from the outset that the virtue of a mere mortal woman was insufficient to receive his prostrations, was born of her as she drew near her end.
When he reached the age of seven, seeking to learn writing, he mounted a goat-drawn carriage and went to the gate of his teacher’s residence.

At that time, as the sages had long since passed away, two characters were missing from a script; when he asked his teacher about them, the teacher could not explain them, which instead stimulated his own resolve.
By the age of ten, his marvelous talent became even more manifest.
The Prince had two cousins who were brothers; the elder was named Devadatta, and the younger was called Nanda.
Although Devadatta possessed extraordinary talent that was naturally difficult to equal, he was arrogant and constantly harbored feelings of envy.
He invited them to the rear garden and provided iron drums as targets; they all drew their powerful bows and shot at them.
Every time the Prince released his arrow, it struck the center and pierced through the drum.
The two men could not match him and considered this a source of shame.
After a long time, he was invited again to engage in hand-to-hand combat before the king, with the stipulation that whoever lost would be drenched with water.
The Prince, being compassionate and benevolent, even when striking his brothers, did not cause them physical pain.
After a long time, the two men again requested Nanda’s assistance.
Nanda went forward and seized the elephant by its trunk, pulling it into the courtyard;
Devadatta, possessed of great strength, hauled it and threw it down.
The Crown Prince smiled and slowly stepped forward to seize the elephant, tossing it over the wall so that no one was killed or injured.
Thereupon, the two men realized they were no match for him;
the King and his attendants further recognized that he was no ordinary man.
When he reached the age of fourteen, he requested the King’s permission to go out on an excursion, desiring to observe the ways of the world.
The King commanded his attendants and the hundred officials to escort him.

As they were just leaving through the eastern gate of the city, the Lord of Heaven transformed himself into a sick man—emaciated in body and swollen-bellied—leaning against the wall by the gate and gasping for breath.
The Crown Prince asked,
"Who is this person?
His servant replied:
"He is ill. "What is meant by being ill?
He replied:

"Generally, all illnesses arise from wind and cold, or heat and cold; this person must have contracted this disease because they failed to regulate their diet and were irregular in their sleeping and rising."
The Prince said: "How bitter it is!
Though I dwell in wealth and honor, my food and drink satisfy my palate, yet I too have no moderation; I shall surely fall ill again—how is this any different from this [suffering]?"
He immediately turned his chariot back, sorrowfully reflecting that all human life is subject to this affliction; how could one escape it alone by means of wealth and power?
He subsequently became so distressed that he refused to eat, thinking to himself that he could not endure such a disease.
The king asked his attendant,
"When the prince went out on his excursion, was he not pleased?
He replied:
"Upon seeing a sick person, he became displeased.
The king immediately increased his retinue of five hundred courtesans to entertain him day and night.
Yet the king’s heart remained filled with sorrow and anxiety, fearing that [the prince] would study the Way.
After several years, his condition having slightly improved, he again addressed the King, saying:
"I have been confined within the palace for a very long time; I wish to go out on an excursion.

The King could not bear to refuse him, so he issued a preliminary decree throughout the kingdom: "The Crown Prince is about to go out; do not allow those who are ill or impure to remain by the roadside."
"The Prince mounted his carriage and went out through the southern city gate.
The Lord of Devas again transformed himself into an old man, with white hair and a hunched back, leaning on a staff and walking with feeble steps.
The Prince asked:"
"Who is this? the servant replied, "An old man."
"What constitutes old age?

He replied, "When one's years are advanced and the faculties have matured, the physical form changes and the complexion fades; food and drink are no longer digested, the vital energy becomes depleted and feeble, and sitting or rising is attended by extreme suffering. With little life remaining, it is therefore called 'old age.'"
The Prince said:
"What joy can there be!
The sun and moon race on, seasons change and years pass; things flourish in spring and wither in autumn and winter. Old age arrives like a flash of lightning—how can this body be relied upon?"

He turned his chariot back and returned, pitying human life for its lack of permanence in youth, and how there is old age and sickness whose pain is unbearable; "I cannot dwell long in this world while being afflicted by such suffering," he thought, and he became distressed and ceased to eat.
The king regretted having sent him out and increased his retinue by five hundred more courtesans to provide him with entertainment.
After several years, his illness slightly improved, and he desired to go out on an excursion again.
The king said:
"Every time you go out for an excursion, you return invariably unhappy; you do nothing but grow thin with anxiety. Why then do you continue to go out?
The Prince replied, "I am merely mindful of that suffering; it will surely diminish as I grow older."
The King issued an edict throughout the kingdom, commanding that no elderly, infirm, or impure persons be allowed along the roadside.
The Prince then mounted his carriage and departed through the western city gate.
The Heavenly Lord again transformed himself into a dead person; the men and women of the household held banners and followed the carriage, weeping as they escorted him.
The Prince asked again:
"Who is this person?"
The servant replied,
"He is a dead man.
[The king asked,] "In what way is he dead?"
He replied:

"Death is exhaustion. Life has its long and short spans; when blessings are exhausted and the life span ends, the vital breath ceases and the spirit departs, and the physical form dissolves and vanishes—therefore it is called death."
"All persons are unified in this way; there is no life that does not end.
The Prince said, "Death is indeed painful; the torment to the spirit is extreme!"
Those born must inevitably encounter the sufferings of old age, illness, and death; that one does not feel burning distress within and is instead forced to confront them—is this not suffering?

I observe those who die: their forms decay and their bodies dissolve, yet the spirit is not extinguished. Following their good or evil deeds, calamity or fortune follows them of its own accord. Wealth and honor are impermanent; the body is but a precarious fortress.
Therefore, the sage constantly regards the body as a source of affliction;
yet the fool clings to it, never reaching satiety until death.
I can no longer undergo birth after death, wandering through the five realms of existence and exhausting my spirit.
He turned the chariot back and returned; pitying that the world was subject to these three sufferings, he was so grieved that he could not eat.
The King became even more displeased and said, "The kingdom is yours;
you should govern the people. Why do you worry about such distant matters as to exhaust yourself with suffering?"
Furthermore, five hundred more court ladies were added to provide him with entertainment.
When the Prince reached the age of seventeen, the King sought to marry him off; though thousands of famous maidens from within the kingdom were selected and examined, none met his approval.
The last daughter was named Gopī; she was so upright, beautiful, and pure that she was the foremost in the world.
Her wisdom and talent surpassed others, and she was fully endowed with propriety and righteousness; she was, in fact, the woman who had sold flowers in her past lives.

Although the Crown Prince had accepted her, he did not have intercourse with her for a long time. The woman, in accordance with the desires of a female, wished to draw near to him, so the Crown Prince said:
"Take some fine flowers and place them between us as we look at them together; do you find them beautiful?"
Gopī then prepared exquisite flowers and wished to approach him.
The Prince said, "Put these flowers away; their sap will stain and soil the bedding."
After a long time, he spoke again:
"If we obtain some fine white cotton cloth and place it between us, would it not be wonderful for the two of us to gaze at it?
His wife immediately prepared the cloth, yet she also harbored a desire for intimacy.
The prince said, "Keep away!
You are defiled; you will surely soil this fine cotton cloth.
The woman did not dare to approach.
The attendants standing by her side all harbored doubts, thinking he was incapable of fathering a son.
The Prince pointed to the Queen’s belly and said,
"Six years from now, you shall give birth to a son."
"Thus he came to possess a body.
Thereupon, the Prince again requested to go out for an excursion.
He went out through the northern city gate, where the Lord of the Devas once more manifested as a śramaṇa, wearing the dharma robes and holding an alms bowl, walking while looking at the ground.
The prince asked,
"Who is this person?
His attendant replied:
“He is a śramaṇa. “What is meant by ‘śramaṇa’?
He replied:

"I have heard that the Way of the śramaṇa consists in abandoning home, wife, and children; renouncing love and desire; severing the six sense-faculties; and maintaining the precepts through non-action. This Way is pure: for one who attains single-mindedness, all myriad evils are extinguished."
The Way of single-mindedness is called Arhatship. An Arhat is a true person;

neither sound nor form can defile them, and neither honor nor rank can humble them. They are as immovable as the earth, already freed from sorrow and suffering, and possess mastery over both life and death.
The Prince said: "Excellent!
Only this is what brings true joy."
He immediately turned his chariot around and returned.

He observed a fast and did not eat, contemplating the purity of the Way; he felt that it was not fitting to remain at home and resolved instead to dwell in the mountains and marshes to refine his essence and practice dhyāna.
Gopī felt doubt in her heart; knowing that he wished to depart, she neither sat nor rose, remaining by his side.
When he reached the age of nineteen, on the night of the eighth day of the fourth month, a deity appeared at the window and, with palms joined, said:
"The time has come for you to go!"
The Prince looked up and replied, "I am closely surrounded by guards;
if I wish to depart, there is no way.
Thereupon, the celestial deity caused his wife and the various female attendants to fall into a deep sleep.

The Prince rose slowly, listened to his wife’s breathing, and observed the various female musicians; they were all like wooden figures, their hundred joints entirely hollow, resembling plantain trees.

Among them were some with disheveled hair leaning against drums, others casting down their burdens and prostrating over lutes; they lay with one another as pillows, their arms and legs hanging to the ground, mucus from their noses and tears from their eyes, while saliva flowed from their mouths.
The lutes, harps, zithers, and flutes lay scattered among the musical instruments; the *xiāoqīng* and mandarin ducks, those who had served as his sentinels, were all lying in a deep and heavy sleep.

The Prince surveyed them all and then turned his gaze upon his wife, beholding her entire form in detail: her hair, nails, marrow, and brain; her bones, teeth, and skull; her skin, flesh, tendons, veins, fat, and blood; her heart, lungs, spleen, kidneys, liver, gallbladder, intestines, and stomach; her excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva. Outwardly she was but a leather bag, and within it was filled with foul matter—not a single thing therein was worthy of wonder;
yet she was forcibly perfumed with incense and adorned with flowers and silks.
It is like a loan that must be returned and cannot be reckoned as lasting long: of a hundred-year lifespan, half is spent lying in bed;
moreover, with much anxiety and affliction, there is but little joy.
Lust destroys virtue and renders one foolish; it is not praised by those Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, or True Persons.
Therefore it is said:
"Greed and lust lead to old age; anger leads to illness; and delusion leads to death."
"Only by setting aside these three things can one attain the Way.

Having reflected thus with single-minded concentration, he rose and gazed at the constellation Puṣya; when the night was already past its midpoint, he saw various devas above him joining their palms and exhorting the Prince to depart.
He immediately called for Chandaka and had him slowly saddle the horse. Drawing up his robes and mounting it, he paced about the courtyard, mindful that opening the gate would produce a sound.

The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, having long known his intention, commanded the spirits and deities to lift the horse’s hooves and support Chandaka as they leaped over the palace walls and proceeded to the royal fields beneath a Jambu tree.
The next day, there was great commotion within the palace; not knowing where the Prince was, thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of horsemen pursued him in an unending stream.
The King himself then went to the fields and saw the Prince from afar, sitting beneath a tree.
The sunlight was scorching and fierce, so the tree bent its branches to provide shade over his body.
The King, startled and awakened by this, realized he was dealing with a divine being; not recognizing him as a mere mortal, he dismounted and prostrated himself.

At that moment, the Prince also stepped forward and bowed, saying: "Since I became a son, I have rarely left the kingdom; now that I have come here for the first time, why has Your Majesty deigned to come all this way? I pray you return at once."
The reason I now wish to leave the world is that, from my own observation, affection is like a dream; the joys of family life must all end in separation.
Greed and desire are a prison, from which it is difficult to escape.
Therefore it is said:

"One obscures oneself with the net of desire and covers oneself with the shroud of attachment; one binds oneself in prison like a fish entering a basket-mouth, awaiting old age and death as a calf seeks its mother's milk."
I have always used this to awaken myself; I vow to seek spontaneity and desire to eliminate all sufferings.
Those who have not yet been delivered, I wish to deliver them;
those who have not yet attained liberation, I wish to liberate them.
"Those who are in distress, I wish to bring peace to;
those who have not yet seen the Way, I wish to cause them to attain it.
Therefore, I desire to enter the mountains to seek my aspiration; once I have attained the Way, I shall return and never forget this vow."
The King, knowing that his resolve was firm, was bewildered and did not know what to say.
He returned to the palace and said to Gopī:
"As my son's heart is pure and as difficult to move as the earth, he takes no pleasure in wealth and honor, nor does he long for the world; he desires only the Way and expects to surely attain it."

"Then the Prince, leaning against a tree branch, saw a plowman tilling the soil; as he turned up the earth, worms emerged and were pecked and swallowed by crows. Moved by compassion for sentient beings who devour one another like fish scales, he thought: 'The unrighteousness of those who cause such harm is ever more severe; they fall into the evil realms after death, and it is most difficult for them to seek escape.'"

Although the pleasures of the devas are joyful, they are nonetheless impermanent; when their merit is exhausted, they feel dread, and when their transgressions arrive, they are terrified. Misfortune and fortune follow one another in succession, and thus the cycle of birth and death endures for a long time.
Observing the human realm and ascending as far as the twenty-eighth heaven, one sees that despite their ultimate nobility, those who lack the Way stand with hell at their very doorstep.
In the abodes of the three evil paths, there are hundreds of forms of excruciating suffering; joy is but fleeting, while sorrow and dread endure for long.
"Between heaven and earth, there is nothing that can be considered extraordinary; I can no longer be deluded by desire.

He immediately rose and mounted his horse, leading Chandaka forward for several tens of li. Suddenly, he beheld the Great Deity of the Five Paths, named Pishun (Benshi), who was preeminently solitary and fierce. He held a bow in his left hand and an arrow in his right, with a sharp sword girded at his waist;

he dwelt at the crossroads of the three paths: the first called the Path of Heaven, the second the Path of Humanity, and the third the Three Evil Paths—this is what the souls of the deceased must pass and behold.
The Crown Prince arrived and asked, "Which path do you follow?
Ben-shi was struck with terror; he cast down his bow, released his arrows, and unsheathed his sword, then hesitated before pointing out the Way of Heaven, saying:
"This path is worth following.
After traveling several dozen li, he encountered two hunters. The Prince thought to himself:
"I have already abandoned my home and am here in these mountains and marshes; it is not fitting for me to wear precious garments like an ordinary man and display the airs of desire."
Thereupon, he removed his precious fur cloak and exchanged it with the hunter for a deer-skin garment.
Arriving before [the city], he dismounted from his horse and sent Chandaka back.
Chandaka knelt down and said:
"Now that I am following Mahādeva, I cannot return alone.

The Prince said, "You may return directly and report to the Great King, as well as offer my thanks to the wife of the householder; I am now seeking the Unconditioned Great Way, so do not worry about me."
He immediately removed his jeweled crown and the garments upon his body, handing them all over to Chandaka.
Thereupon, the white horse knelt down and licked his feet, its tears falling like a string of pearls.
Chanda wept with grief, crying as he followed the road.
Looking back at the Prince, he saw that he had already donned a deer-skin garment and departed in altered attire.
"Chanda returned on foot, leading the horse, and throughout the palace and the capital, there was none who did not feel deep sorrow."
Gopī wept and threw herself down at the foot of the palace steps, saying:
"I looked toward the Prince as one who thirsts for a drink; why do you now return alone and empty-handed with the horse?"
He stepped forward, embraced the horse’s neck, and asked where the Prince was.
Chandaka said, "The Prince first addressed the Great King and took leave of the Queen; he now seeks the Unconditioned Great Way, so do not grieve for me."
Gopī wept and said:
"How cruel is my fate! To have lost my lord while still living! Where is he now?"
"What were you seeking when you went out?
He patted the horse's back and said, "The Prince rode you out; why have you come back alone?"
The people of the entire kingdom could not help but sob;
the King, overcome with grief and sighing, his tears flowing profusely, said to Gopī:
"As my son has realized, the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death are indeed a great affliction."

This was a divine man; on the day of his birth, the Supreme Deity descended in person, and ten thousand deities stood guard around him, with auspicious omens and radiant signs such as had never been seen in the world.
The seer Ārāḍa prophesied:
"If you do not delight in the world but renounce your home to follow the Way, you will surely become a self-enlightened Buddha and shall deliver and liberate the myriad people."
"Now that you have taken leave to study the Way, is this not natural?

The King, wishing to resolve Gopī’s thoughts, was himself moved with emotion; he immediately selected several thousand men of noble and virtuous standing from within the kingdom, choosing five who were particularly burdened by many descendants, and presented them before her.
The King said:
"You all have elder sons who embrace their grandchildren; do you alone feel joy?

I have an only son who has never left my gate. If he were to abandon me one day and travel far into the deep mountains, through dangerous ravines and valleys, amidst the perils of fortune and misfortune, cold and heat, hunger and thirst—who would know of him?"
"I trouble you five men; each of you must send one son to search for him. Once he is found, he shall be attended by you.
Should any of you abandon the quest midway and return, I shall exterminate your clans and lineages."
Thereupon, Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya and the other four men received their orders and pursued the Prince.
When they reached the deep mountains, they attended upon him for several years.
The Prince did not speak with them, but continued his travels as before, ascending mountain ridges and crossing deep valleys by climbing over thickets.
The five men were distressed by this and said, "This is merely a madman; what path could he have?
He travels without choosing his way—how can we follow him?"
"If we were to return home, the King would destroy our family; it would be better to stay here.
At the place where the five men stayed, there was a fine spring, and sweet fruit was never lacking.
"The Prince departed on his own, traversing famous mountains and passing through the realm of Magadha.
King Bimbisāra, having gone out to hunt, saw the Prince from afar as he traveled through the mountain marshes."
He immediately went with the elders and great ministers to pursue and see him.
The King said:

"The Crown Prince was born amidst many wonders, and his physical marks are brilliant and distinct; he shall rule over the four quarters of the world as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin). The people of the four seas look up with reverence, hoping for the arrival of the divine treasures."
"Why have you abandoned the celestial throne to seek solace among the mountain thickets?
There must be some extraordinary insight behind this.
I wish to hear your resolve."
The Prince replied:

"As I perceive it, all things within heaven and earth—humans and beings alike—are born and must die; there are three bitter sufferings, and the pains of old age, sickness, and death cannot be escaped."

I reckon that this body is a vessel of suffering, fraught with immeasurable anxiety and fear. If one dwells in honor and favor, there arises arrogance and indolence, as well as a greedy pursuit of pleasure; thus the world is afflicted by calamity. This is what I loathe, and therefore I wish to enter the mountains to cultivate my resolve.

The elders said, "Now, old age, sickness, and death are the natural constants of the world; why do you alone worry in advance, abandoning your noble title to live in seclusion and obscurity, thus wearying your physical form—is this not difficult?"
The Prince replied:
"As you all say, one should not worry in advance.
Suppose I were to become king; when old age arrives and sickness comes, should the time for death arrive, would there be anyone who could take my place and undergo this misfortune?"
Since there is no one who can take one’s place, how could one not worry!

Though the world may have compassionate fathers and filial sons whose love penetrates to the very marrow of their bones, when the time of illness and death arrives, they cannot substitute for one another.

Thus, when suffering reaches this false body, even if one occupies a high position with six kinds of relatives by one’s side, it is like setting a candle before a blind man; what benefit is it to one who has no eyes?

I observe all conditioned phenomena and see that they are entirely impermanent; all are transformations and not real. Pleasure is slight while suffering is abundant; the body is not one's own possession; the world is empty and void, and it is difficult to dwell there for long.

When things are born, they must die; when affairs are accomplished, they must fail; where there is security, there is peril; where there is gain, there is loss. All phenomena are in constant turmoil, yet all must ultimately return to emptiness.
The spirit is formless; when it is restless and turbid, it lacks clarity. It undergoes the perils of death and birth not merely once, but repeatedly.
Yet, because of greed and desire, it is shrouded within the net of delusion and submerged in the river of birth and death, unable to awaken.

Therefore, I wish to concentrate my mind on the purity of the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpyasamāpattayaḥ*), transcend form, extinguish ill-will, sever the seeking of thoughts, and remain in emptiness without partiality toward this or that. This will be to return to the source and revert to the root; once I have begun to uproot [delusion], if I may obtain what I desire, then I shall attain great peace.
King Bimbisāra said with joy:
"Excellent! The Bodhisattva’s resolve is sublime and rare in this world; he will surely attain the Way of the Buddha. I pray that you deliver me first."
The Crown Prince departed in silence.
As he was about to cross the Nairañjanā River, a celestial deity stilled the current so that its bed became temporarily dry.
After the Crown Prince had crossed the river and traveled several tens of *li*, he encountered three brahmins, each with his own disciples, dwelling separately by the side of a stream.
When questioned about his path, he declared of himself:
"I serve Brahmā and revere the sun and moon; I daily perform fire sacrifices, holding that only water is pure."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"This is merely the path of birth and death!

Water is not always full; fire does not remain hot for long; when the sun rises, it moves on; when the moon is full, it wanes. Since the Way resides in purity and emptiness, how could water ever cause the human mind to become pure?"

Grieved by this, he departed; as he walked, he gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), contemplating universally that sentient beings—aged, decrepit, and utterly ignorant—are not exempt from the pains of illness and death, and he desired to bring them liberation so that they might unify their minds, thereby giving rise to a mind of compassion (*karuṇā*).

Compassionately pitying all beings who suffer from hunger, thirst, cold, heat, gain, loss, transgressions, and hardships, he desires to bring them peace and security so that they may unify their minds, and thus gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
Reflecting that all in the world encounter the afflictions of sorrow, suffering, and fear, he desires to bring them tranquility and unify their minds, thereby giving rise to a protective heart.

Desiring to deliver those born within the five realms and eight difficulties—who are deluded, obscured, and ignorant, failing to see the Right Path—one resolves to bring them salvation so that they may attain the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). With a unified mind, one neither rejoices upon encountering the good nor grieves upon meeting with evil; one abandons the eight worldly concerns—gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure—and remains unshaken by them.
Having already traversed the deep mountains and reached a secluded and tranquil place, he saw a peepal tree with a pure and serene vista in all directions.
He thought to himself:
"I have already abandoned my home to dwell here in these mountain marshes; it is not fitting that I should continue to groom my hair as an ordinary person does."

Because one harbors thoughts of combs, brushes, baths, and perfumes, one loses the intention for pure precepts, right concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; this is not the purity of the Path, but rather it defiles pure conduct.
"I shall become a śramaṇa according to the dharma of a bodhisattva.
A celestial deity presented him with a razor, whereupon his beard and hair fell away by themselves; the deity then accepted them and departed.

The Bodhisattva immediately gathered blades of grass and spread them upon the ground. He sat upright in a cross-legged posture, joined his palms, closed his eyes, and made a solemn vow with single-minded concentration:
"I shall let my flesh and bones wither and rot here; until I have attained Buddhahood, I will never rise.
A celestial deity offered him food, but he refused it once and for all.
The deity then commanded his attendants to produce hemp and rice from themselves, so that he might consume one grain of hemp and one grain of rice daily to sustain his vital energy.
He sat upright for six years; his body became emaciated until skin and bone were joined together. He was profoundly pure, tranquil, and serene, remaining silent and single-minded.

Internally, he contemplated *ānāpāna*—first counting, second following, third stopping, fourth observing, fifth returning, and sixth purifying. His will wandered through the third and fourth stages and emerged from the twelve gates, without any distracted thoughts.
His supernormal powers are subtle and wondrous; having abandoned desires and unwholesome dharmas, he is free from the five hindrances and no longer accepts the five sensual pleasures.

All evils are naturally extinguished, his mindfulness and discernment are clear and distinct, and his thoughts are non-active. It is like a strong man who has defeated his enemies; his mind is thus purified, and he accomplishes the practice of the first dhyāna.
The mind opened and understood itself, turning away from the impulses of desire; there was no evil to be amended, nothing more to be calculated or observed, and discursive thought had already ceased.
It was like a spring at the summit of a mountain, where water wells up from within and flows outward in abundance; neither mountain torrents nor seasonal rains can find a way to enter.
Maintaining tranquility and serenity while guarding the One, one remains joyful and unwavering, thereby accomplishing the practice of the Second Dhyāna.

Furthermore, discarding the state of joy, one perceives only the absence of passion; external likes and dislikes cannot enter at all, nor do they arise internally. With the mind upright and the body at ease—like a lotus root in water where the flower is closed and yet to open, its roots, stem, branches, and leaves all saturated with water—one perceives the True through purity, thereby accomplishing the practice of the Third Dhyāna.
Abandoning the notions of suffering and pleasure, free from the perceptions of sorrow and joy, the mind neither relies on the wholesome nor clings to the unwholesome, remaining exactly in the middle.

Like a person who has bathed until clean and is covered with a fresh, fine white cotton cloth—pure both within and without, stainless inside and out—the breath ceases of its own accord; in this profound stillness and immutability, one accomplishes the practice of the fourth dhyāna.

It is like a potter who prepares clay until it is supple and free of grit; whatever vessel he fashions, through diligent application, there is nothing he cannot accomplish, for he has attained a concentrated mind.

Without abandoning great compassion, wisdom, and skillful means, he thoroughly masters the essential subtleties and penetrates the practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path. These he cycles again and again, free from all defilement, with his mind directed toward the three gates:
first, he inclines toward emptiness, contemplating cessation without distraction, neither grasping nor relinquishing.
Second, one is oriented toward the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*), wherein the mind remains fixed and does not arise, and one no longer conceives of likes or dislikes.
Third, one is oriented toward wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), taking no pleasure in the three realms and no longer giving rise to suffering.
He immediately attained three kinds of liberation:
first, freedom from desire; second, freedom from hatred; and third, freedom from delusion, such that he was no longer hindered by any obstacles.

Thereupon, the sixth *Nirmāṇarati* Heaven, where the Māra of the heavens resided, beheld the Bodhisattva’s purity and lack of desire, his diligent meditation without slackening. Distressed in heart, his food and drink became tasteless, and he could no longer enjoy music or dance, thinking:
"This Way will be perfected, and he will surely greatly surpass me.
Before he attains Buddhahood, I must destroy his resolve for the Way.
The Māra-son Sāta came forward and admonished his father, saying:

“The Bodhisattva’s conduct is pure and peerless throughout the three realms; having attained spontaneous supernormal powers, billions of Brahmās and devas all go to pay him homage and serve him. This is not something a celestial king should attempt to thwart; do not give rise to evil and thereby diminish your own merit.”
The Mara King would not listen;
he summoned three jade maidens—first named Desire Consort, second named Delighting Him, and third named Pleasing Sight—and sent them to corrupt the Bodhisattva’s resolve.

The three daughters were all dressed in garments of fine gauze and adorned with celestial incense, necklaces, and precious jewels; they employed extremely seductive and artful words, seeking to disturb his mind.
"The Bodhisattva’s mind is pure, like a lapis lazuli bead that cannot be defiled.
The three women spoke again, saying, "Your virtuous majesty is most profound and revered by all the devas; it is because you deserve offerings that the heavens have presented us to you."

"We are fond of purity and refinement, and we are in the prime of our youth; among the celestial maidens, none is more beautiful than I. I pray that I may rise at dawn and retire at night to serve by your side."
The Bodhisattva replied:

"You possess merit from past lives that has allowed you to receive this celestial body; yet, failing to contemplate impermanence, you have acted with such seductive artifice. Though your physical form is beautiful, your heart is not upright."
It is like a painted vase filled with foul poison, which one carries about only to bring about one's own ruin.
What is so extraordinary about this? Merit cannot endure for long; through lustful evil and unwholesome conduct, one destroys one's very foundation.
Upon death, you shall surely fall into the three evil realms and take the forms of birds and beasts; it will be difficult to escape them.
You people have disturbed the right mind; you are not of pure lineage. You have come here as leather bags filled with excrement—what is the purpose of this?
"Go! I have no use for you.
Thereupon, the three jade maidens transformed into old women, unable to restore themselves.

The Mara King became even more incensed and summoned further spirits and ghosts, totaling one hundred and eighty million beings; he caused them all to transform into the shapes of lions, bears, brown bears, tigers, rhinoceroses, elephants, dragons, oxen, horses, dogs, pigs, monkeys, and apes, in numbers beyond description.

They had the heads of insects and the bodies of humans; they possessed the bodies of venomous snakes with the heads of soft-shelled turtles and six eyes; some had a single neck with many heads, fanged teeth, and talons like spikes; they carried mountains and spat fire, surrounded by thunder and lightning, clutching spears and halberds.
The Bodhisattva’s heart of loving-kindness remained unshaken and fearless; not even a single hair moved, and his radiant countenance became even more beautiful.
The ghostly army retreated and dispersed, unable to draw near.
The Māra King came forward in person to challenge the Buddha with these words:
“Bhikṣu, what do you seek by sitting beneath this tree? You take delight amidst the thickets and forests where venomous beasts dwell;
Clouds arise, fearsome and pitch-black— Are you not startled by the celestial Māras surrounding you?”
"In ancient times there was the True Path practiced by the Buddhas; serenity is supreme for eliminating ignorance.
That city is most excellent, a treasury filled with the Dharma; seeking this seat, I shall decisively overcome the King of Māra."
"You shall become a king who turns the golden wheel, with the seven treasures arriving spontaneously as you govern the four quarters;
the five sensual pleasures you enjoy shall be peerless, yet in this place there is no path for you to enter the palace."
"I observe that the height of desire is like swallowing molten copper; I would abandon a kingdom as if it were spittle, having no greed for it.
Even attaining kingship brings the anxieties of old age and death; depart from this profitless talk and do not speak such delusions."
"Why do you sit so peacefully in the forest and speak with such grandiosity, abandoning your kingdom, wealth, and status to dwell in empty seclusion?
You do not see me raising my fourfold army—eighty billion elephants, horses, and infantry!"
I have already seen the faces of monkeys, apes, and lions; the forms of tigers, rhinoceroses, venomous snakes, and boar-demons.
All brandish swords and blades, seize halberds and spears, leaping and bounding with roars that fill the air.
"Even if hundreds of millions of divine warriors were to assemble here as Māras like you,
with arrows, blades, and fire-attacks falling like wind and rain— I shall not rise until I have first attained Buddhahood."
Māra has a fundamental vow to cause me to retreat, yet I too have sworn that I shall not return empty-handed;
now, as this field of merit is like that of a Buddha, it shall be known therein who attains victory!
"I once practiced joyful giving throughout my entire life, And thus presided over the six heavens as a Mara King;
O Bhikṣu, you know my past meritorious deeds, But who can testify to my own claim of being 'immeasurable'?"
“I, in former times, made my vow before Dīpaṃkara, Receiving the prediction that I would become the Buddha Śākyamuni;
Because anger and fearful thoughts are exhausted, I sit here; With mind fixed and certain of liberation, I shall destroy your army.”
The Buddhas whom I have served are many; I have constantly bestowed wealth, treasures, clothing, and food upon others.
Your benevolence and precepts have accumulated merit as vast as the earth; therefore, you are liberated from conceptualization and free from all suffering and hardship.
The Bodhisattva, by the power of his wisdom, extended his hand and touched the earth, saying, "This one knows me.
At that moment, the entire earth shook with a great roar, and Māra and his retinue fell down, overturned.
The Demon King was defeated and despondent at his loss; bewildered, he retreated and sat down, drawing lines upon the ground before him.
His son then enlightened him, and his mind finally awakened; he immediately returned of his own accord to repent for his transgressions:
"I shall no longer employ weapons of war; instead, I will practice universal compassion to repel demonic enmity."
The world employs weapons that stir the hearts of men, yet I treat all sentient beings with equanimity.
Though an elephant or horse may have been tamed, its former habits will surely arise again;
but if one attains the ultimate taming of the Buddha-nature, one is as benevolent as a Buddha who has already tamed them.
"Ten million devas beheld the Buddha subduing the hosts of Māra; With patience he tamed them, and the thoughtless enemies surrendered of their own accord.
The various devas rejoiced and arrived offering flowers; The non-Dharma king was defeated, and the Dharma King triumphed."
Fundamentally derived from the power of equanimity and wisdom, this wisdom can instantly dispel all inauspiciousness;
it can even cause enemies to become disciples—one should pay homage to the realization of the four immeasurables.
His face is like the full moon and his bearing is composed; his fame reaches the ten directions and his virtue is like a mountain.
The features of the Buddha’s image are difficult to find a peer for; one should prostrate before this immortal who delivers the world.
