“The Bodhisattva’s pure conduct accumulated over kalpas reached the ultimate point of great compassion; his Way was settled and spontaneous.
Through the power of forbearance, he subdued the demons; the demonic armies retreated and dispersed, yet his concentrated mind remained as it was before.”

Without relying on intellectual deliberation, and free from thoughts of sorrow or joy, during the first watch of this night, he attained the *ṛddhi* of knowing past lives; he personally knew his own destiny throughout countless kalpas, perceiving all the successive transformations of his spirit and the immeasurable number of bodies he had successively assumed. He recognized and understood them all.

At the second watch of the night, he attained the second *ṛddhi-vidyā*, whereby he knew the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings—their good and evil, their misfortunes and blessings, and the destinies of their births and deaths.

At the third watch of the night, he attained the third *ṛddhi-vidyā*; with his outflows exhausted and fetters untied, he realized for himself the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) long practiced in former lives—namely, the concentration of energy, the concentration of desire, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of precepts—and thereby attained the power of transformation.

Their desires are fulfilled according to their wishes without further deliberation; they can fly through the air and multiply a single body into hundreds, thousands, up to billions or countless numbers, then merge them back into one;
they can pass through the earth and penetrate stone walls as if they were nothing; they appear from one direction and vanish or emerge from below like ripples on water;
they can emit water and fire from their bodies, walk upon water, and travel through space without sinking or falling.
Sitting or reclining in mid-air like a bird in flight;
standing, one could reach the heavens and touch the sun and moon with one's hand;
and desiring it, one’s body could stand level and reach as far as the Brahma-heaven of Sovereignty.

His eyes can see through all things, his ears can hear with penetrating clarity, and his mind fully knows everything in advance; regarding the physical actions, verbal expressions, and mental thoughts of devas, humans, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and all classes of crawling and wriggling creatures, he perceives them all through seeing, hearing, and knowing.

He fully knows all those who have lust and those who are free from lust; those with anger and those without anger; those with delusion and those without delusion; those with craving and those without craving; those with great aspirations and conduct and those without great aspirations and conduct; those with internal and external practices and those without internal and external practices; those who recollect what is wholesome and those who do not recollect what is wholesome; those with a unified mind and those without a unified mind; and those with a liberated mind and those without a liberated mind. He knows them all completely.

“The Bodhisattva contemplates and perceives the five realms—devas, humans, hells, animals, and hungry ghosts—and clearly distinguishes, one by one, their parents, brothers, wives, and children from previous lives, as well as their ancestral lineages and names.

From one lifetime through ten lifetimes, and across hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of countless lifetimes, up until the time when heaven and earth were destroyed and lay desolate for an eon, and the time when an eon first formed and sentient beings arose, he is able to know the internal and external names, clothing, food, suffering and joy, the length of life, death here and birth there, and the successive destinations throughout ten eons, a hundred eons, and even up to thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of countless eons.”

Starting from the very beginning, one discerns and knows all successive bodies—birth, growth, aging, and death; beauty and ugliness of form; the wise and the foolish; suffering and happiness; and everything within the three realms.

He saw that the spirits of people each follow their own karma as they are reborn within the five realms: some fall into hell, some fall among the animals, some become ghosts or spirits, some are born in the heavens, and some enter human form. Among them, some are born into families of noble rank, wealth, and pleasure, while others are born into families of low status, poverty, and meanness. He understood that all sentient beings are either obscured by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*):
first, form; second, sensation; third, perception; fourth, mental formations; and fifth, consciousness—and that they all habitually indulge in the five desires.
The eye craves forms, the ear craves sounds, the nose craves fragrances, the tongue craves flavors, and the body craves tactile sensations;
led by craving and desire, whether for wealth or for sensuality, one longs for peace and happiness, and from this arise the roots of all evils, which lead from evil to suffering.
One who can sever the habit-energies of craving and does not follow a lustful mind—even one as small as a hair—and who practices the Eightfold Path, shall extinguish all suffering.
It is like having neither fuel nor fire; this is called the unconditioned path that transcends the world.

“The Bodhisattva knows for himself that he has already cast off the roots of evil and is free from lust, anger, and delusion; birth and death have been eliminated, the seeds and roots have been severed, no further stumps remain, what was to be done has been accomplished, and wisdom has reached its consummation.”
When the morning star appeared, he attained great enlightenment, realizing the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way, and became the Most Perfectly Awakened One.
He attained the eighteen dharmas of a Buddha, including the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses.
The eighteen qualities of a Buddha refer to the period from his attainment of Buddhahood until his parinirvāṇa:
first, no loss of the path; second, no empty speech; third, no forgetting of his resolve;
fourth, no lack of tranquility in mind; fifth, no manifold perceptions; sixth, no lack of clear observation; seventh...
1. No decrease in aspiration; 2. No decrease in vigor; 3. No decrease in mindfulness; 4. No decrease in concentration; 5. No decrease in wisdom; 6.
No decrease in liberation; 7. No decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation; 8. No decrease in vigor; 9. No decrease in meditative absorption;
10. No decrease in wisdom; 11. No decrease in liberation; 12. No decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation; 13. Complete knowledge and vision of past lives; 14. [Knowledge of] future lives.
14. He fully knows and sees matters of the past; 15. He fully knows and sees matters of the present life; 16.

He surveys the conduct of the bodies of all beings and transforms them based on what he originally knew; 17. He surveys the conduct of the speech of all beings and transforms them based on what he originally knew;
18. He surveys the conduct of the minds of all beings and transforms them based on what he originally knew.
These are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Regarding the "ten powers":

first, the Buddha fully knows and perceives the profound, subtle, hidden, and remote, as well as what is possible and what is impossible, discerning them clearly and exactly as they are; this is the first power.
Second, the Buddha fully and clearly knows the actions performed in the past, present, and future, the stages of those actions, and the retributions received therefrom; this is the second power.
The Buddha discerns each and every distinct thought of devas, humans, and sentient beings; this is the third power.
The Buddha fully knows the various kinds of languages of sentient beings as well as the languages for transcending the world; this is the fourth power.
The Buddha fully understands the immeasurable and diverse dispositions of the world; this is the fifth power.
The Buddha is able to manifest meditative absorption, liberation, concentration, and practice to eliminate the toil and strife of the multitude; this is the sixth power.
The Buddha knows the bonds of desire and knows the essential requirements for the practice that leads to liberation from those bonds; this is the seventh power.
The Buddha’s wisdom is like the ocean and his skillful words are immeasurable; he recollects all past lives and everything experienced therein; this is the eighth power.
The Buddha’s divine eye is pure; he sees beings die and their spirits take birth, experiencing retribution according to their conduct—whether good or evil, calamity or fortune.

This is the ninth power. The Buddha’s outflows are exhausted; he is free from all further fetters and attachments. With his spirit of true wisdom, he has personally realized and witnessed [the truth], fully mastering the practice of the Way. Having accomplished what was to be done, there is no further rebirth; his wisdom is clear and discerning. These constitute the ten powers of a Buddha.
"The four fearlessnesses are as follows:
regarding the Buddha’s divine wisdom and perfect enlightenment, there is nothing he does not know. Yet, out of delusion and ignorance, some might say:
'The Buddha has not fully realized all things.'"
As for the Brahmā and the assembly of sages, none were able to debate the Buddha’s wisdom; thus he walked alone without fear, possessing the fourfold fearlessness.
The Buddha had exhausted all outflows and knew them completely, yet the deluded and confused spoke among themselves, saying, "The Buddha’s outflows are not yet exhausted."
"Because even among the Brahma-heaven sages and holy ones, none were able to debate the Buddha’s resolve, he walked alone without fear; this is the second fearlessness.
When the Buddha preached the sutras and precepts and they were recited and practiced throughout the world, the ignorant and deluded said to one another:
'The Buddha's sutras can be suppressed.'"
"Because even among the Brahma-heaven sages and holy ones, none are able to refute or disparage the Buddha’s true scriptures, he walks alone without fear; this is the third fearlessness.
When the Buddha manifests the meaning of the Path, his words are true and essential, capable of delivering one from suffering and distress. Yet the ignorant and deluded say to one another:
'The Buddha cannot deliver one from suffering.'"
"Because even the Brahmā assembly of noble sages was unable to debate the Buddha’s True Path, he traveled everywhere without fear; this is the fourth fearlessness.
Having attained meditative concentration and possessing all-knowing insight, the Buddha sat and reflected to himself:
'This reality is truly subtle and wondrous, difficult to know and difficult to clarify; it is exceedingly hard to attain.'"
It is high without being surpassed and vast beyond limit;
it is deep without a bottom and profound beyond measure;
it encompasses heaven and earth in its greatness and penetrates the infinitesimal gaps in its subtlety.
In the past, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he prophesied that I would become a Buddha named Śākyamuni;
now I have indeed attained this.
For incalculable eons, I have sought it through diligent toil and hardship, and only just now have I finally achieved it.

Reflecting upon his own past lives, he considered all that he had practiced: compassion, filial piety, benevolence, and righteousness; ritual propriety, reverence, sincerity, and trustworthiness; uprightness and the preservation of goodness; cultivating the sages with an empty mind; gentleness and purity of intent; and practicing the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom.
They cultivate the four immeasurable minds—compassion, pity, joy, and equanimity;
they nurture all sentient beings as if looking upon their own infants;
and they serve all Buddhas, accumulating immeasurable merit.
"Through diligent toil over many kalpas, I did not hope for its reward, yet now I have attained it all myself.
He joyfully declared:
"I now realize that the Buddha is most supreme; having abandoned lust, he is pure and free from outflows."
He who can lead all beings, whose followers are surely filled with joy;
for whom the retribution of merit is swift, and whose sublime vows are all fulfilled;
who out of compassion has quickly attained supreme tranquility—I shall now depart into Nirvana.

"When the Buddha first attained the Way, he knew for himself that his body was light and emaciated from eating little; he rose slowly and entered the water to bathe. When he finished and wished to step onto the bank, a deva pressed down a tree branch so that he could grasp it and emerge, whereupon he proceeded to go beneath the tree."
There were five hundred green pheasants that flew in, circled the Buddha three times, and departed.

Furthermore, there was the daughter of an elder who had recently married and made a vow that, should she give birth to a son, she would prepare a congee of a hundred flavors to sacrifice to the mountain and tree deities.
Later, she gave birth to a son. Overjoyed, she immediately prepared some gruel and placed it in a golden bowl; when her daughter poured out the gruel, neither the cauldron nor the ladle was soiled.
The girl’s reverence and esteem increased further, and she went into the mountains with several other women. Upon seeing a beautiful tree, she sent a maidservant ahead to clear the area.
When the maidservant arrived, she saw the Buddha and, not knowing what deity he was, returned to report to the girl:
"There is a deity sitting beneath a tree.
The woman had her maidservant carry a bowl of gruel made from a hundred flavors upon her head and place it before him; she then knelt long and offered the food along with the golden bowl.
The Buddha said, "Since you have been able to harbor such benevolent intentions, you shall surely attain blessings in this present life and realize the Truth.

The women bowed from afar and withdrew. After the Buddha had finished eating the gruel, he reflected that when the three previous Buddhas first attained the Way, there were those who offered them food of a hundred flavors along with superior golden bowls such as these; they are all currently in the possession of the Dragon King Muṇḍin.

The Buddha then cast his bowl into the water; it naturally flowed upstream for seven *li*, landing atop the three bowls previously placed before him. The four vessels were stacked together, appearing as one.
The Dragon King was filled with joy, knowing that there was yet another Buddha.
For seven days, the Buddha remained in meditative concentration, neither moving nor wavering.
A tree deity thought to herself:
"The Buddha has newly attained the Way and has sat joyfully for seven days; as yet, no one has offered him food. I shall seek out people and have them provide a meal for the Buddha.
At that moment, there happened to be five hundred merchants passing by one side of the mountain; their carts and oxen all stumbled and could not move forward.

Among them were two great men, one named Trapusa and the other named Bhallika; terrified, they returned with the crowd to the tree deity to request blessings. The deity manifested a radiant form and said:
"In this world there is a Buddha, here in the realm of Uruvilvā by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, to whom no one has yet offered food."
"If you all can fortunately first cultivate a benevolent mind, you will surely obtain great merit.

When the merchants heard the name of the Buddha, they were all filled with joy and said, "The Buddha must be uniquely and most venerable, one revered by the heavenly deities; he is certainly no ordinary being."
He then mixed the flour with honey, went together to the foot of the tree, and prostrated himself before the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:

"The Dharma of the Buddhas of antiquity for pitying those who offer alms is that they always carry an alms-bowl; it is not fitting that I should receive food directly from the hands of others as do the practitioners of other paths."
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, knowing from afar that the Buddha would require alms bowls, arrived together upon Mount Aṇḍa in the time it takes a person to bend or extend their arm;
as they had intended, four bowls spontaneously emerged from within the rock—fragrant, pure, clean, and free of impurity.
The Four Heavenly Kings each took a bowl and returned together to present them to the Buddha, saying:
"We pray that you will have compassion for these merchants and cause them to obtain great merit.
We now have iron bowls; later, the disciples shall use them for their meals."

The Buddha thought, "If I take only one bowl, it will not satisfy the intentions of the other three. He then accepted all four bowls, stacked them in his left hand, and pressed them down with his right hand, merging them into a single bowl while allowing the four rims to remain visible.
The Buddha accepted the parched grain and honey, and addressed the merchants:
"You should take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma. Since there will soon be a community of bhikṣus, you should also take refuge in them in advance."
They all immediately accepted the instruction and each took the three refuges three times.
After the Buddha had risen and finished eating at another location, he offered a prayer of blessing for the merchants, saying:
"May that which has been given as alms cause those who eat it to obtain sufficient strength."

May the donor’s family, from generation to generation, fulfill their aspirations; may they obtain beauty and strength, receive honor and joy, remain peaceful, healthy, and free from illness, and live out their full natural lifespan;
may no malevolent spirits or demons be able to harass or approach them;
and by virtue of their wholesome intentions, may the foundation of their merit be firm.
May all benevolent spirits and deities constantly provide protection;
may they reveal the stages of the Path and grant favorable opportunities for success;
may they prevent misfortune and ensure that no further hardships or afflictions arise.
If a person possesses right view and acts with faith, joy, and reverence;
if they are pure and free from regret, bestowing gifts upon those who possess the Way and its virtue;
their merit and fortune will increase ever greater, becoming increasingly superior as it develops, bringing auspiciousness and nothing but benefit.
The sun, moon, five planets, twenty-eight lunar mansions, celestial deities, and ghost kings will constantly follow, protect, and assist you;

the Four Great Heavenly Kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the East, Virūḍhaka of the South, Virūpākṣa of the West, and Kuvera of the North—will distinguish and reward the virtuous, and shall protect you all so that you do not encounter untimely calamities.
Should you possess a wise mind, diligently study the teachings, revere the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, abandon all evils, and refrain from self-indulgence.

One experiences auspiciousness in the present; by planting merit one obtains merit, and by practicing the Way one attains the Way. Because you have previously seen the Buddha and served him with single-minded devotion, you shall thereby attain the foremost merit.
"One shall obtain blessings in this present life, swiftly attain liberation through the vision of the Truths, enjoy wealth, happiness, and long life, and personally reach Nirvana.

At that time, the flour-milk was cold and wind arose within the Buddha’s abdomen. Śakra, knowing this immediately, arrived at the borders of Jambudvīpa and took a medicinal fruit called harītakī. He came before the Buddha and said, "This fruit is fragrant and delicious;
it may be consumed, for it most effectively eliminates internal wind."
The Buddha then ate it, and the wind was immediately dispelled.
He proceeded to the waterside of the blind dragon Mucilinda; having sat down for seven days, he neither breathed nor sighed.
Light shone into the water, and the dragon’s eyes were opened; he regained his former consciousness and, beholding the radiance of the Three Buddhas, his sight was restored.
The Dragon King, filled with joy, bathed himself and emerged from the water bearing exquisite incense, sandalwood, and *sugandha*.
Beholding the Buddha’s marks and signs, whose radiance was like flowers upon a tree, he circumambulated the Buddha seven times, his body remaining forty *li* away from the Buddha’s perimeter.
The dragon had seven heads, which he spread out to cover the Buddha above.
Desiring to shield [the Buddha] from mosquitoes, gadflies, cold, and heat, as well as the seven days of torrential rain, the dragon remained single-mindedly without hunger or thirst.
When the rain ceased after seven days, the Buddha attained awakening. The dragon transformed himself into a young practitioner, dressed in fine garments, and prostrating before the Buddha, he asked:
"Has the Buddha not been cold? Has he not been hot? Has he not been troubled by mosquitoes and gadflies?"
The Buddha then replied:
"It has been long since I have been in a secluded place; how joyful is the merit of contemplating the Path!
What I formerly wished to hear, I now know it all—how joyful!"
To be untroubled by those [afflictions] is a joy; to be able to bring peace to sentient beings is a joy.
To transcend the world and extinguish the three poisons is a joy; to attain the Buddha’s nirvāṇa is a joy.
To be born in this world and behold a Buddha is a joy; to hear and receive the teachings of the Dharma is a joy.
To meet with Pratyekabuddhas and true persons is a joy;
Not associating with the foolish and being free from evil people is a joy;
Possessing the discernment to distinguish the true from the false and knowing how to trust the Right Path is a joy.
The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"You should further take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus.
He then received the three refuges.
Among all the various animals, these nāgas were the first to see the Buddha.
By means of his supernormal powers, the Buddha moved his seat to a stone chamber; there, he reflected upon his original vow, desiring to deliver sentient beings.
He reflected:
"Birth and death fundamentally arise from the twelve links of dependent origination; because phenomena arise, there is birth and death;
if phenomena cease, then birth and death are exhausted."
Because one acts thus, one obtains this; because one does not act thus, this ceases.

All sentient beings take the mind as their spirit; it is profound and obscure, vague and formless. From within itself, it gives rise to perceptions and thoughts, following which it undergoes embodiment.
The body has no permanent master, and the spirit has no permanent form; the spirit-mind undergoes transformations, being turbulent and turbid, difficult to purify.
Arising and ceasing by themselves, they never rest;
one thought departs and another arrives,
like bubbles upon water— where one drop vanishes, another immediately reappears.
As for the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, where the nine types of spirits dwell, all are bound to consciousness and cannot escape suffering;
being in a state of profound obscurity and lacking self-awareness, this is called delusion (*moha*), whereby one knows not the essential path.
The Way is supremely subtle; it is empty, still, and free from thought, and thus cannot be known by the ordinary worldly mind.
Among the ninety-six types of worldly paths and arts, each person believes in their own practice—whom can one call deluded?
All beings delight in birth and seek security; they crave desires and relish flavors, and take pleasure in sounds and sights. Therefore, they are unable to find joy in the Buddha-way.
The Buddha-way is pure, empty, and devoid of anything substantial;
for ordinary people reckon that the body and all things cannot be maintained forever. Were one to preach this to them—that all under heaven is suffering—[they would not believe it].
"Emptiness is nothingness; who could believe it?
It is merely a source of withered suffering for me.
Thinking thus, he wished to remain silent and not preach the Dharma to the world, and so he entered into meditative concentration.
The Buddha emitted a light from between his eyebrows that shone upward, illuminating the seven heavens.
Brahmā, knowing that the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, thought with sorrow:

"All within the three realms will suffer long-term decline; they shall never know the Dharma for transcending the world. After death, they will surely fall again into the three evil paths. When will they ever be liberated?"

It has been a long time since there was a Buddha in the world; a Buddha is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower. Now, for the sake of the devas and humans, I shall entreat the Buddha with compassion to cease preaching this sutra.
He immediately spoke to Śakra, who brought down the celestial musician Pañcaśikha to the stone cave.
Just as the Buddha was emerging from his meditative absorption, Pañcaśikha played the lute and sang.
The words of the hymn say:
"Listen to my song of the Ten Powers; having cast off the hindrances, he dwells in tranquil meditation.
His light penetrates and illuminates the seven heavens, and the fragrance of his virtue surpasses that of sandalwood."
The Supreme Deity has arrived with wondrous grace, sighing in admiration and longing to behold the Honored One;
Brahmā and Śakra, bearing respectful intent, bow their heads in prostration, desiring to receive his teaching.
The fundamental vows and practices of the Buddha were cultivated through diligent effort for a hundred kalpas.
With the four immeasurables and great generosity, the ten directions receive vast grace;
Through pure and stainless upholding of precepts, they compassionately and gently protect all beings;
With courageous resolve, they enter meditative wisdom, and with great compassion, they spread the sutras for deliverance.
Having accumulated ascetic practices for countless eons, his meritorious achievements are perfected today;
through the power of morality, patience, concentration, and wisdom, he has shaken the earth and captured Māra.
His virtue universally covers heaven and earth, and his divine wisdom surpasses that of the spirits and sages.
His marks and signs are peerless; his eightfold voice resounds through the ten directions.
His resolve is loftier than Mount Sumeru; its purity and subtlety are beyond description.
Forever free from lust, anger, and delusion, he is no longer subject to the afflictions of old age and death.
Only out of compassion, may you arise from your meditative absorption; take pity on all devas and humans.
Open the treasury of the Dharma’s jewels and spread the precious nectar of your grace.
Cause them to be liberated from sorrow and fear, so that those in peril and distress may find peace.
May those who are deluded see the right path, and may those with false doubts behold the true teaching.
May all beings aspire to it with joy, desiring to hear and receive it without weariness;
may you reveal the deathless Dharma and extend its transformation infinitely.
The Buddha, knowing this entirely in his mind, arose from his meditative absorption.
Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since time immemorial, I have only just now seen a Buddha again."
The devas rejoice and leap for joy, desiring to hear the Buddha-dharma; you should preach the sutras for the sake of the world, and we pray that you do not enter parinirvāṇa.
Sentient beings are ignorant and dark, lacking the eye of wisdom; please bestow your compassionate guidance so that they may attain liberation.
Among the various devas and humans, there are many who are virtuous and good, who delight in the Way and find it easy to understand, and who are also diligent and capable of receiving the precepts.
For those who fear the hells and the three evil realms, I pray that you open the treasury of the Dharma and manifest the nectar of immortality; those who receive it will surely be many.
When there is no Buddha in the world, I see other practitioners who, possessed of the three poisons, compose scriptures according to their own whims.
People still study those insincere teachings; how much more so should they study the pure teachings of the Buddha, which are free from lust, anger, and delusion?
"I pray that the Buddha will preach the Dharma, so that sentient beings may hear the Way of ultimate sincerity.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Brahmā! Wishing to extensively bestow peace, to rescue all the world, to comfort, benefit, and bring relief to it, and to joyfully cause its liberation—I contemplate the world:

how beings, through craving and attachment to sensual desires, fall into the suffering of birth and death; few are able to awaken to the fact that this [suffering] fundamentally arises from the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions grasping; grasping conditions becoming; and becoming conditions birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and mental distress."
To possess existence is a great affliction; the spirit follows after craving and thus undergoes the cycle of birth and death.

Those who wish to attain the Way must sever greedy craving and extinguish sensual desires, remaining in a state of non-action and non-arising. Thus, ignorance ceases; when ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; when volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; when consciousness ceases, name-and-form cease; when name-and-form cease, the six sense bases cease; when the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; when contact ceases, feeling ceases; when feeling ceases, craving ceases; when craving ceases, clinging ceases; when clinging ceases, existence ceases; when existence ceases, birth ceases; and when birth ceases, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and mental distress—all these great afflictions—are utterly exhausted. This is called attaining the Way.
Only the Buddha awakens to this, which is subtle and difficult to clarify.
Indeed, this purity, free from deluded thoughts, cannot be known by the minds of worldly ordinary people.

Among the various arts and paths of the world, numbering ninety-six kinds, each has its own object of worship: some serve Heaven and Earth, the sun, moon, and the five planets; others serve water, fire, ghosts, spirits, dragons, and deities. All of them delight in life and seek security, craving desires and flavors, and taking pleasure in sounds and sights; therefore, they cannot rejoice in the Buddha-way, do not hear the Buddhist sutras, and do not know the essential Dharma.

Ordinary people have different views; they calculate that their bodies and the myriad things can exist eternally. If one were to explain it to them: that which is seen by the eyes, the myriad things, are impermanent; having a body is entirely suffering; the body is not a self; it is empty and possesses nothing; and kinsmen and family members are all not what belongs to a person.
"Right words appear to be contrary; who could believe them?
I am suffering from withered misery, and it would be better for me to attain Nirvāṇa; therefore, I wish to remain silent.
Brahmā spoke again:
"Since countless kalpas, beings have wandered in birth and death within the world; The Buddha’s sutras are exceedingly difficult to hear.
From the Buddha who dwells in the world and can deliver those at the furthest limit, I have now attained my vow—something rare among men.
Most honored and supreme, with none to compare to the Buddha, Therefore, I bow my head in prostration."
The world has long been bound and attached, dwelling in darkness; now the One of Ten Powers has arisen, his divine wisdom immeasurable.
He shall open the treasury of the Dharma and bestow the light of wisdom, illuminating all devas and humans so that they may attain understanding.
Since the Buddha can deliver all beings, I therefore vow to take refuge in him.
From the first resolution of your mind, you vowed to act for the sake of those suffering; through tireless humility, you have accumulated merit and perfected your vows.
Ignorance, old age, and death are a long-standing decline, truly pitiable; you shall bestow the medicine of the Dharma to rescue all from their ailments.
There is no one whose compassion surpasses the Buddha’s; therefore, I prostrate and entreat you.
The Buddha, having granted his consent to Brahmā, thought:
"Who should be the first to be delivered?
Formerly, my father the King sent five men to attend upon me; they are now in the mountains."
He then returned by the same way. When the five men saw the Buddha, they said to one another, "Be careful not to rise when this man approaches.
But when the Buddha arrived, all five rose and, without realizing it, paid him homage.
Then the Buddha said:
"How is it that you hold your minds without firmness?
You were just told not to rise; why do you prostrate?"
The five men did not respond, but wished to become his disciples.
The Buddha then stroked their heads with his hand and ordained them as śramaṇas.
They returned to the foot of the Bodhi tree and sat down, each reflecting in meditation.
The Buddha further reflected:

"In this region there is Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa—of great brilliance and valor, possessing a noble reputation, whom kings, officials, and commoners all serve together—he dwells with five hundred disciples on the banks of the Nairañjanā River."
"I wish first to transform and enlighten him so that he may understand, rejoice in, and have faith in the Buddha-dharma;
only then will others follow and learn from him.
He then went to follow him.
When Kāśyapa saw the Buddha, he immediately rose to greet him and praised him, saying:
"How fortunate! Welcome, Great Wayman; have you been well?"
The Buddha then replied:
"Freedom from illness is the foremost benefit; contentment is the foremost wealth; virtuous friends are the foremost intimacy; and the unconditioned is the foremost peace."
Kāśyapa asked, "What command do you have for me?
The Buddha said:
"I wish to request one thing; if you will not be angry, I would trouble you to lend me your fire chamber for a single night.
He replied, "I do not begrudge it."
"Within it dwells a venomous dragon; I fear it may harm you.
The Buddha said, "Do not worry."
"The dragon will not harm me.
He requested this repeatedly, up to three times.
Kāśyapa said:
"However, as the Great Way-man’s virtue is lofty, it would be most excellent if he could dwell within.

The Buddha then washed himself and entered the fire chamber; taking grass, he spread it upon the ground and sat down for a short while. The venomous dragon, filled with rage, emitted smoke from his body;
the Buddha likewise manifested his spiritual power, emitting smoke from his own body.
The dragon became greatly enraged, and fire issued from its entire body;
the Buddha also manifested his spiritual power, and fire issued from his body as well.
The dragon’s fire and the Buddha’s light both blazed intensely together; the stone chamber was completely ablaze, with flames and smoke billowing forth like the scene of a wildfire.
Kāśyapa rose in the night and, observing the constellations, saw that the fire chamber was ablaze.
He sighed and said, "Alas!
This Great Śramaṇa was so handsome; it is a pity he did not follow my words and has now been destroyed by this poisonous fire."

The Buddha, knowing his intention, used his supernatural powers within that room to extinguish the dragon’s poisonous wrath, subdue its body, and transform it so that it was placed within his almsbowl.
Kāśyapa was terrified and hurriedly ordered five hundred disciples, each holding a jar of water, to go and extinguish the fire;
yet each jar of water instead became another fire, and the master and his disciples grew even more afraid, all exclaiming:
"Alas! Alas!"
"I have killed this great śramaṇa.
At dawn the next day, the Buddha went out carrying his alms bowl filled with the dragon.
Kāśyapa was struck with wonder and asked, "Great Way-man, are you still alive?"
"What is in the vessel?
The Buddha replied,
"Indeed, it is simply myself who am alive."
"The one within this bowl is the venomous dragon, whom all people fear and dare not enter the chamber.
Now that he has been subdued, he has already received the precepts."
Kāśyapa, believing himself to have attained the Way, considered the Buddha not to be truly enlightened.
He turned to his disciples and said, "This great śramaṇa possesses extreme supernatural powers; yet even so, he has not reached the Way, for he does not equal me, who has attained arhatship!"
The Buddha again moved closer to Kāśyapa and sat beneath a tree. During the first watch of the night, the Four Heavenly Kings descended together to listen to the Buddha preach the sutra.
The radiance of the Four Kings was as bright as a blazing fire.
Kāśyapa rose at night to observe the omens and saw four fires beside the Buddha.
The next morning, he went to inquire:
"Does the Great Wayman also practice fire-worship?"
The Buddha said,
"I do not serve the fire. He asked:
"Last night there were four fires here; what was that?
The Buddha said, "Last night the Four Heavenly Kings descended to listen to the sutra; it was their radiance."
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses supreme spiritual power.
Nevertheless, because he has not yet attained the Way, he is not equal to me who have attained arhatship!"
"The Buddha was staying under a tree on the second day. That night, Śakra came down again to listen to the Buddha preach the sūtra.
The radiance of Śakra’s body greatly increased the brightness."
Kāśyapa rose at night to observe the omens of the heavens; seeing that the firelight beside the Buddha was twice as bright as the four fires from the previous day, he thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa continues his practice of tending the sacrificial fire."
The next morning, he went again to inquire:
"Great Way-man, have you not been tending a fire?
The Buddha said:
"No, it was not. Yesterday Śakra, Lord of Devas, descended to listen to the sutra; these were his rays.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed divine and holy;
nevertheless, he has not yet attained the Way, for he is not equal to me who have attained arhatship!
Later in the night, the seventh Brahmā Heaven descended once more to listen to the sutra.
The radiance of Brahmā was twice that of Śakra.
Kāśyapa rose at night to observe the omens and saw that the light of the fire had become even more brilliant and magnificent.
The next day, he asked:
"Does the Great Way serve fire?
He replied,
"It does not serve fire!"
“Last night the firelight became increasingly bright and great;
why was that? The Buddha said, “Last night Brahmā descended to listen to the sutra; it was his radiance.”
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed miraculous; yet he has not attained the Way, and thus he is not my equal, who has attained arhatship!"

“Kāśyapa had five hundred disciples, each of whom tended three fires, totaling fifteen hundred fires. When they lit them at dawn, the fires would not ignite at all. Finding this strange, they informed their teacher.”
The teacher said,
"I suspect this is the work of that great śramaṇa.
He then went at once to question the Buddha.
"I have five hundred disciples, each of whom tends fifteen hundred fires. This morning, when we lit them, none of the fires would burn.
Could this be the doing of some great practitioner of the Way?"
The Buddha said,
"Do you wish for the fire to burn?
He asked this up to three times.
He said,
"I wish to make it burn.
The Buddha said:
"You may go; the fire shall ignite.
As soon as he spoke, they all ignited.
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed possessed of supernatural powers, yet he has not attained the Way; he is not my equal, who have already attained arhatship!
Kāśyapa himself tended three fires; when he lit them the following morning, they would not catch fire.
He thought to himself,
"This must also be the doing of that great śramaṇa," and immediately went to question the Buddha.
"I personally tend three fires; this morning I attempted to kindle them, yet they would not ignite at all.
Could this be the doing of some great practitioner of the Way?
The Buddha said:
"Do you wish for the fire to burn?
He asked this up to three times.
[The man] replied:
"I wish to make it burn.
The Buddha said, "You may go; the fire shall burn."
At his voice, they all burst into flame.
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed miraculous; however, he has not yet attained the Way, and thus is not my equal, who has already attained arhatship!"
"After the fire had burned, Kāśyapa wished to extinguish it, but he was unable to do so.
His five hundred disciples and all those who served the sacrificial fires joined him in their efforts to extinguish it, yet it would not go out at all."
Everyone said,
"This was done by the Great Śramaṇa.
Then Kāśyapa went to inquire of the Buddha.
"The fire has already been kindled; can it not now be extinguished?
The Buddha said, "Do you wish for it to be extinguished?"
He replied,
"I wish to cause them to cease.
The Buddha said:
"You may go; the fire shall be extinguished.
As soon as he spoke, it was extinguished.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"Although this great śramaṇa possesses spiritual power, he is not equal to the true realization of the Way that I have attained!
Kāśyapa then went to inform the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Great Man of the Way will remain here; there is no need for him to travel further. I shall personally provide him with food."
He immediately returned and instructed his household to prepare a fine meal for the following day;
once the seats had been arranged, he went in person at the time of the meal to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Go ahead; I shall follow shortly.

As soon as Kāśyapa had departed, in the time it takes a person to bend and stretch their arm, the Buddha traveled eastward across the realm of Pūrvavideha for several thousand *koṭis* of *yojanas*, where he took the fruit of a tree called jambu, filled his alms bowl to the brim, and returned.
Before Kāśyapa had arrived, the Buddha was already seated upon his bed.
When Kāśyapa arrived later, he asked:
"Great Way-man, by which path have you come?"
The Buddha said,
"Just as you departed, I went east to the land of Pūrvavideha and took some jambu fruits, which are fragrant, delicious,
and fit for eating. He then took them and ate them.
After the Buddha had finished his meal and departed,
Kāśyapa continued to think:
"Though this great śramaṇa possesses spiritual powers, they are not equal to the truth of my own Way!"
On the following day at mealtime, Kāśyapa again invited the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Go ahead; I shall follow shortly."

As soon as Kāśyapa had departed, the Buddha traveled southward for many thousands of li to the very edge of the Jambudvīpa continent, where he gathered harītakī fruits and returned with his alms bowl filled to the brim.
Before Kāśyapa had returned, the Buddha was already seated upon his bed.
When Kāśyapa arrived, he asked:
"By what cause have you come here first?"
The Buddha said, "Just as you departed, I traveled south to the very edge of this world-system and gathered a harītakī fruit; it was both fragrant and delicious.
He then took it and ate it.
After the Buddha had finished his meal and departed,
Kāśyapa continued to think:
"Although this great śramaṇa possesses supernatural powers, they are not equal to the truth of my own Way!"
The next day, Kāśyapa again went to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Go ahead; I shall follow shortly."

As soon as Kāśyapa had departed, the Buddha traveled westward to the realm of Aparagoyanī, a distance of several thousand billions of *li*, where he took an *āmalaka* fruit. He returned with his almsbowl filled to the brim and arrived before Kāśyapa, sitting upon the bed.
Kāśyapa arrived later and asked the Great Wayman,
"From where have you come?
The Buddha said:
"Shortly after you departed, I went west to the land of Godānīya and took some āmalaka fruits, which are fragrant, delicious, and fit for eating.
He then took them and ate them.
After the Buddha had finished his meal and departed,
Kāśyapa thought again:
"Although this great śramaṇa possesses spiritual powers, he is still not equal to the true Way of my own!"
The next day, Kāśyapa again invited the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Go ahead; I shall follow shortly."
Kāśyapa looked back, but suddenly the Buddha was nowhere to be seen.

By means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the Buddha had traveled north to the realm of Uttarakuru, many hundreds of billions of *li* away, where he took naturally grown non-glutinous rice, filled his bowl, and returned; arriving before Kāśyapa, he sat upon the bed.
Kāśyapa arrived later and asked,
"Great Way-man, from where have you come?
The Buddha said:
"From the land of Uttarakuru in the north, take this matured non-glutinous rice; it is delicious, fine, and fragrant. Try eating some of it.
Having finished his meal, the Buddha departed.
Kāśyapa thought again:
"Although this great śramaṇa possesses supernatural powers, he is still not equal to the truth of my Way!
On the following day at mealtime, the Buddha took his bowl and went to Kāśyapa’s house in person, where he received food and returned.
Having finished eating in a secluded place, the Buddha thought of washing and rinsing his mouth.
Knowing the Buddha’s intention, Śakra, Lord of Devas, descended immediately and pointed to the ground with his finger; water gushed forth, forming a pool for the Buddha to use.
In the late afternoon, Kāśyapa was wandering among the assembly when he saw a spring of water. Marvelling at it, he asked the Buddha, "By what cause has this come to be?
The Buddha said:

"Having received your meal this morning and finished eating here, I thought of washing and rinsing my mouth. Śakra, Lord of the Devas, pointed at the ground and caused water to gush forth; you should name this 'Finger-pointed Pond' (Aṅgārasthāpana)."
Kāśyapa thought again:
"Although this great śramaṇa possesses such spiritual power, he is still not equal to the truth of my Way!
The Buddha returned to the foot of the tree and saw some discarded, tattered rags on the path; he picked them up, intending to wash them.
The Heavenly Lord, knowing the Buddha’s intention, immediately went to Mount Aṇa, where he selected a fine, level stone and brought it to the edge of the pond, saying to the Buddha:
"This may be used for washing clothes."
When the Buddha wished to dry his robes, the Heavenly Emperor again went to fetch six square stones and provided them for drying.
Kāśyapa saw two fine stones by the side of the pond and asked again:
"By what cause have these come to be?"
The Buddha said,
"I wished to wash my robes and also to dry them, so the Lord of Devas went to Mount Aṇā to fetch this stone for me.
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa may indeed possess supernatural powers, yet his Way is not as true as mine!
On a subsequent day, after the Buddha had finished bathing in the Indrakīla Pond, he wished to emerge but found nothing to grasp.
On the bank of the pond there was a tree named Kāśa, which was exceptionally large and beautiful; it naturally bent down toward the Buddha, and the Buddha climbed out by grasping its branches.
When Kāśyapa saw the tree bending down to provide shade, he marveled at it and questioned him again.
The Buddha said, "I entered the pond to bathe, and upon emerging, there was nothing for me to grasp; therefore, the tree deity bent it for me.
Kāśyapa thought again:
"Although this great śramaṇa possesses spiritual powers, he is still not equal to the truth of my Way!
At that time, the King of Magadha, along with his officials and people, came to Kāśyapa’s abode for the seasonal festival, where they enjoyed themselves for seven days.

Kāśyapa thought to himself: "Kāśyapa Buddha is divine and possesses sacred wisdom; if the people see him, they will surely all abandon me to serve him instead. It would be best for him to depart for seven days."
The Buddha, knowing his intention, remained hidden for seven days.
On the following day, Kāśyapa thought again:
"Recently I had a festival, and there was a great deal of leftover food. It would be a joy to have the Great Śramaṇa come and partake of it!"
The Buddha, knowing this from afar, arrived immediately.
Kāśyapa said joyfully, "How wonderful that the Great Way-man has come! I was just now wishing to make offerings to you."
"Why did he not appear for seven days during that interval?
The Buddha said:
"During that interval, the King was meeting with his officials and people for seven days; you thought to yourself: '..."
"This great śramaṇa is divine and wise; if all these people see him, they will surely abandon me together to serve him. It would be pleasant for seven days if he were made to depart."
"Therefore I departed.
Because you now think of me, I have returned.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa indeed knows the minds of others!
Nevertheless, his Way is still not as true as mine!
At that time, Kāśyapa’s five hundred disciples were all splitting firewood; each raised an axe, yet none could bring it down. Alarmed, they went together to inform their teacher.
The teacher said,
"This is the doing of that great śramaṇa.
He then went at once to question the Buddha.
"My disciples were just now splitting firewood together, but all their axes have been raised and will not come down.
The Buddha said, "You may go; the axes shall descend."
The axe fell immediately.
After it had fallen, the axe stuck fast to the firewood; he tried to lift it but could not. He went again to inform the Buddha:
"Just now the axe fell, and yet it will not budge."
The Buddha said, "You may go;
now I shall cause the axe to lift.
Immediately, it lifted up and could be used.
Kāśyapa thought again:
"Though this great śramaṇa possesses supernatural powers, he is still not equal to the true path of my own!

At that time, the waters of the Nairañjanā River flowed swiftly and rapidly; by means of his natural supernormal power, the Buddha cut off the flow and caused it to stand still, making the water rise up in a barrier higher than a person's head, with the riverbed exposed as dust was stirred up, through which the Buddha walked.
Fearing that the Buddha might be swept away by the waters, Kāśyapa immediately joined his disciples and boarded a boat to search for him.
Kāśyapa saw that the water had been cut off in its path and dust was rising from the center, where the Buddha was walking between the two banks.
Kāśyapa called out, saying,
"Great Way-man, are you still alive?
The Buddha said:
"However, I shall sustain myself.
He then asked the Buddha,
"Do you wish to board the boat?"
The Buddha said,
"Very well. Then the Buddha thought:
"Now I shall manifest my spiritual power to cause your mind to submit.
He then passed through the bottom of the boat from within the water, leaving no trace of penetration.
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed miraculous, yet he is not as [accomplished] as I, who have already attained arhatship!
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"You are not an arhat, nor do you know the truth of the Way."
"Why do you falsely claim to be noble?

At this, Kāśyapa was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end; realizing he lacked the Way, he immediately prostrated himself and said, "The Great Master is truly divine and sagely, for he knows my innermost thoughts."
"Is it possible for me to receive the precepts and scriptures from a Great Way practitioner and become a śramaṇa?
The Buddha said, "Go back and inform your disciples; it would be even better to inform them."
"You are a great elder, one upon whom the entire kingdom relies for guidance. Now that you wish to study the Great Way, can you know it all by yourself?
Kāśyapa accepted this instruction and returned to inform his disciples:
"Do you understand? Do you understand?"
"What my eyes have seen, my mind has now come to believe and understand; I shall shave off my hair and beard, don the dharma robes, receive the Buddha’s precepts, and become a śramaṇa.
Where do you wish to go?"
The five hundred disciples said:
"All that we know is due to the kindness of our Great Master; what the Master honors and trusts must certainly not be false. We pray that we may all follow him and become śramaṇas."

Thereupon, the master and his disciples stripped off their furs and coarse garments, took their water jars, staffs, sandals, and all implements for tending the sacrificial fire, and cast them all into the water.
Together they went to the Buddha, prostrated themselves, and addressed him, saying:
"Now we, five hundred disciples, possessing a mind of faith, wish to leave our homes, shave our hair and beards, and receive the precepts of the Buddha."
The Buddha said:
"Very well!
Let all the śramaṇas come."
Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples had their hair and beards fall off naturally, and they all became śramaṇas.
Upaka Kāśyapa had two younger brothers:
the next was named Nadīkāśyapa, and the youngest was named Gayākāśyapa.
Each of the two younger brothers had two hundred and fifty disciples, whose dwellings were situated in rows along the riverbank.
They saw that the robes, utensils, and all the fire-worship implements of the brahmins were all being carried away by the current.
The two younger brothers were struck with alarm, fearing that their elder brother and his five hundred disciples might have been harmed by evil men or swept away by the great flood.
They immediately set out with five hundred disciples, traveling upstream against the current.
Seeing that his elder brother and his disciples had all become śramaṇas, he asked in wonder:
"My elder brother is one hundred and twenty years old; his wisdom is lofty and far-reaching, and he is revered by the king, the officials, and the common people alike."
In my mind, I considered my elder brother to be an Arhat; yet now he has abandoned the path of the brahmin to study the dharma of the śramaṇa—this is no small matter.
Is it not because the Buddha alone is great, and his Way is superior?
Kāśyapa replied,
“The Buddha’s Way is most supreme, and his Dharma is immeasurable.
Although I have studied worldly learning, I have never encountered one who has attained the divine wisdom of the Way like that of the Buddha.”
The sutras and precepts therein are exceedingly pure; I have now witnessed his compassionate deliverance of sentient beings through three modes of teaching:
first, the power of meditative concentration and supernormal faculties, wherein transformations occur spontaneously;
second, wisdom, by which he knows the fundamental intentions of others.
"Third, the Way of the Sūtras is correct practice, providing medicine according to the illness.
The two younger brothers each looked back at their disciples and said,
"Where do you wish to go?"
The five hundred people together raised their voices in unison, saying:
"We wish to be like the Great Master.
They then all prostrated themselves, seeking ordination as śramaṇas.
The Buddha said,
"Very well! All you śramaṇas, come here."
The two younger brothers and five hundred disciples all shaved off their hair and beards, immediately following behind the Buddha and becoming śramaṇas once more.
The Buddha thus came to have one thousand śramaṇas, who together went to the grove of trees in the county of Vārāṇasī and sat down.
The disciples of the Buddha were all formerly brahmins; for their sake, the Buddha manifested supernatural transformations:
first, flying through the air; second, preaching the sutras; and third, providing instruction and admonition.
When the disciples beheld the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, there was none who did not rejoice; they prostrated themselves and received his teachings with devotion.
*The Sūtra on the Auspicious Response of the Prince’s Original Enlightenment*, Scroll Lower.
